Crossing the Chasm at Khaai Hydel Systems

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Go-to-Market & Launch · Case40

1. The night before

Sunday, 27 September 2026, twenty past eleven. Rain came off the Bhabar over Nainital Road, and the third-floor office of Khaai Hydel Systems in Haldwani was empty but for Leela Nautiyal, co-founder and chief product officer. Three documents were open: a 94-page tender from Girvaan Renewables for a fleet platform covering thirty-four small-hydro plants and three grid-scale battery sites, due at 5 p.m. on Friday, 16 October; an estimate from Bengaluru putting the work at 83 engineer-months; and a note from Toronto arguing that the pipeline everyone had quoted for a month was arithmetically meaningless.

At half past seven on Monday she was due on a call with the founders and a board observer, set early to catch Toronto before midnight and New Jersey before ten, expected to bring a recommendation: bid as written, decline, or do something nobody had yet named. Khaai had 300 paying customers, ₹9.24 crore of annual recurring revenue and ₹19.60 crore in the bank against a net burn of ₹1.05 crore a month — a little over eighteen months of runway, ending around March 2028. The Series B thesis required ₹25 crore of ARR by 31 March 2028, and every path there ran through customers Khaai had never served. Four capable people had read the same numbers and reached four different answers, and Leela could not find the mistake in any of them.

2. How Khaai got here

Suchit Negi and Leela Nautiyal registered Khaai Hydel Systems in March 2018 above a tyre shop in Haldwani. Suchit had spent nine years commissioning small-hydro plants across Kumaon and Garhwal; Leela had built telemetry software in Bengaluru and come home. Their answer was deliberately small. A retrofit gateway — the Khaai Box — clamped onto existing turbine and switchyard instrumentation, pushed readings over a 4G SIM to a multi-tenant cloud, and put generation, penstock pressure, silt load and fault alerts on a phone. At ₹18,000 a unit and ₹1.15 lakh per plant per year, a promoter could sign without a board or a procurement committee. Word travelled the Himalayan circuit faster than any campaign, and by September 2026 Khaai's software sat on 448 of the roughly 1,200 commissioned projects in India below 25 MW, about 37 per cent of that fleet.

One decision from that period now governed everything. In February 2021 the founders resolved — minuted, and the minute was Leela's — to build cloud-only and protocol-light: no on-premise deployment, no native IEC 61850 substation modelling, one account per plant. It was the right call for the customer they had. It also meant that when a buyer asked for an air-gapped instance inside its own control-room network, speaking the protocol its switchgear already spoke, the honest answer was that the product could not, and the road to it ran in quarters.

A second decision compounded the first. In July 2022, short of field coverage west of the Yamuna, Khaai signed a five-year reseller agreement with Pashaan Controls, a Chandigarh automation house with vans across Himachal and Jammu. Pashaan took 30 per cent of subscription revenue on plants in those states and, in a clause nobody argued about, a right of first refusal on any fleet-scale opportunity in India, running to 30 June 2027.

3. The industry

Roughly 5 GW of Indian capacity sits in hydro projects under 25 MW, most owned by promoters with one or two plants, with tariffs set by bodies such as the Uttarakhand Electricity Regulatory Commission and dispatch through state load despatch centres into a grid coordinated by Grid Controller of India. Above that long tail sits a different industry: NHPC, SJVN, Tata Power, JSW Energy, Greenko and a dozen state generation companies. These do not buy software from a promoter's phone. They run pre-qualification rounds, demand conformance with the Central Electricity Authority's cyber-security guidelines, ask for ISO 27001 certificates and three references of comparable scale, and write liquidated damages into contracts. Their automation comes from ABB, Siemens and L&T.

Two forces were pushing the industries together. Storage was one: SECI and state tenders had put grid-scale batteries beside renewable assets, and every site needed state-of-health analytics neither the hydro vendors nor the battery makers supplied well — which is what Khaai Cell was launched for in February 2026 at ₹6 lakh per site per year. Regulation was the other. In April 2026 the CEA tightened cyber-security conformance for entities interfacing with load despatch centres; Khaai read it, as did most of the market, as applying above 25 MW. In August the authority clarified that fleets counted by portfolio, and work filed under “enterprise, later” became a condition of bidding.

The exposure was not only Indian. Fjordline Energy AS, a Bergen operator with 41 plants in Vestland, had offered an eighteen-month paid pilot on eight plants worth about ₹38 lakh, on an audit overlapping the Indian work by perhaps three-fifths but requiring European data residency.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Khaai reached 100 customers in October 2021 and 208 by March 2025, almost entirely through referral. Three that looked like fleets signed between March 2024 and June 2025 (Exhibit 6), and internally they were proof Khaai could serve the mainstream: a fleet customer was a long-tail customer multiplied.

That belief did not survive delivery, though the evidence took two years to sit in one place, which Yuvraj Kandpal finally did on 12 September 2026. All three overran their quotes badly, and what consumed the time was not features. It was equipment Khaai had never seen, control-room policies forbidding outbound connections, an IT team demanding a security review Khaai had no documentation to answer, and, in Himachal, a nine-to-fourteen-hour drive to each site.

The second error concerned the battery module, conceived as an upsell to the installed base. Of the four battery sites live in September 2026, three were bought by organisations that had never bought the hydro product, and in each the decision sat with the EPC contractor. Lohit Bora's note of 26 September observed that Khaai had not extended its market but entered a second one, with a different buyer and possibly a different chasm.

The third was Pashaan Controls, treated until now as coverage. On 19 September, Saumil Bisht learned that Pashaan had pre-qualified for the same tender in its own name, at a price he believed was about ₹20 lakh below Khaai's. Whether its right of first refusal reached a tender Khaai had been invited to went to outside counsel on 22 September; no answer had come by Sunday night.

5. The people

Leela owns the recommendation and has never said aloud that the February 2021 minute now blocking the company was hers. Seven others hold positions.

Suchit Negi — Co-founder & Chief Executive, Haldwani. Wants the full bid: one fleet logo converts the state gencos, and the long tail is a good business but not a venture-scale one. Unsaid: Deodar has hinted that without a marquee reference the next round is flat.
Ekansh Dhasmana — VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Produced the 83-engineer-month estimate and privately thinks it optimistic by 30 to 40 per cent; his pod's attrition ran at 19 per cent. Unsaid: two of his four senior engineers hold outside offers.
Yuvraj Kandpal — Head of Field Delivery, Rudrapur. Insists the binding constraint is vans and technicians, not protocols; his bonus tracks SLA attainment, at 91 against a 95 per cent target. Unsaid: he has been quietly declining Himachal installations to protect it.
Elakshi Uniyal — Head of Compliance, Kotdwar. Holds that CEA conformance and DPDP Act obligations are a licence to bid, not features: without them Khaai is out of every state tender by 2028. Unsaid: she has not established whether Girvaan's own certification would cover a hosted Khaai instance.
Saumil Bisht — Head of Enterprise Sales, Edison, New Jersey. Believes the referral engine has run out of road; three-fifths of his variable pay rides on new enterprise contract value. Unsaid: he set Exhibit 5's probabilities himself, and has told no one Pashaan is underbidding him.
Lohit Bora — Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Argues the only defensible Segment C forecast is Exhibit 2's base rate, and that weighted pipelines in a segment with three lifetime wins are storytelling. Unsaid: his churn model flagged eleven accounts at risk in FY26; nine renewed.
Sohini Semwal — Chief Operating Officer, Girvaan Renewables, Rudrapur. Would prefer Khaai to win; her board mandated a three-vendor shortlist and a conformance clause she did not draft. Unsaid: that board approved only ₹1.20 crore of digitisation spend across three years, and Annexure C reserves Girvaan's right to take the platform in-house after year three.

7. Voices

Ekansh Dhasmana to Leela Nautiyal, direct message, 12 September

“83 is what I can defend in a room. What I believe is 110 to 120, because their security review will find things and I do not know what. And if we fork an on-prem variant, in two years we maintain two products with one team.”

Yuvraj Kandpal, delivery review, Rudrapur, 18 September

“Forget the protocol. Bhatoli is fourteen hours from Rudrapur in a good month, and the tender says four-hour response for a Severity 1. Either we station two people and a vehicle in Himachal, about ₹34 lakh a year, or we sign something we cannot do.”

Lohit Bora, memo to the leadership team, 26 September

“I am not arguing against the deal, I am arguing against the number. Exhibit 5 says ₹55.31 lakh; our own history says ₹9.12 lakh. That gap is not rounding, it is the whole decision.”

Sohini Semwal, clarification call with Khaai, 23 September

“The conformance clause is not negotiable, our lenders wrote it. The dates are. The commercial envelope is less negotiable than you think. And do not assume the incumbent is only bidding hardware.”

Sigrid Halvorsen, Fjordline Energy AS, Bergen, email of 24 September

“We can start on eight plants in January and say so publicly. But our audit is IEC 62443 and our data stays in the EEA. If you are already doing this for an Indian customer, perhaps 60 per cent carries across; if not, we ask you to do it twice.”

8. The options, as Leela currently frames them

  1. Bid in full and fund the ₹199.2 lakh build. Commit the eight-engineer pod for roughly 10.4 months and treat compliance as the investment that opens Segment C permanently. The exposure: Exhibit 6's overruns repeating at fleet scale, Ekansh's private 110 to 120 engineer-months being the real figure, and the roadmap for 297 Segment A and B customers stopping for a year.
  2. Decline and deepen the long tail. Hold the architecture, push ARPU with the battery module, and take the rest of the fleet, protecting a base on 81 and 74 per cent gross margins and a 35 per cent win rate. The arithmetic is uncomfortable: ₹9.24 crore to ₹25 crore of ARR on Segment A economics needs about 876 more single-plant customers at ₹1.80 lakh each, against a universe of roughly 1,200 projects of which Khaai touches 448.
  3. Go through Pashaan Controls. Let Pashaan prime the bid and supply the control-room stack, Khaai the analytics layer: 30 per cent or more of revenue and the customer relationship surrendered, none of the compliance build incurred. It preserves cash and coverage, concedes the mainstream customer, and rests on a partner now bidding against Khaai.

The framing has three soft joints. It treats the build as indivisible when Exhibit 3 is six separable workstreams, only three load-bearing for go-live. It treats Girvaan as the beachhead when the ₹1.20 crore envelope and Annexure C make it a poor one, and when Fjordline's eight plants buy a reference for a fraction of the money. And it treats the battery line as an attachment to the hydro business, when three of its four sites came from a buyer Khaai has never sold to.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The response is due at 5 p.m. on Friday, 16 October 2026; award is expected in November, the first twelve plants live by 30 June 2027, full conformance evidence by 31 December 2027. Dussehra and Diwali fall in between. Yugank Karki, the board observer from Deodar Growth Partners, wants one further thing by the March board: a written statement of where Khaai's ceiling is, which nobody has produced.

Money: ₹19.60 crore of cash, ₹1.05 crore of monthly net burn, runway to about March 2028, and a Series B thesis of ₹25 crore ARR by 31 March 2028 against ₹9.24 crore today. People: 118 staff — 26 engineers in Bengaluru, 54 in Haldwani, 22 in field delivery at Rudrapur, 9 in Kotdwar, 7 elsewhere. Regulation: CEA conformance, DPDP Act obligations, customer-side deviation settlement exposure, EEA residency if Fjordline proceeds. Contracts: Pashaan's 30 per cent Himachal share and unresolved right of first refusal; liquidated damages capped at ₹16.38 lakh; a ₹1.20 crore envelope against a ₹163.8 lakh proposal; and Annexure C.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1, 2 and 6, what changes between a Segment B and a Segment C customer — a product gap, a service gap, a credibility gap, or three at once?
  2. Exhibit 2's footnote and Exhibit 5's probabilities cannot both be right. What is the honest base rate for a Segment C win, and what would you need before raising it?
  3. Which of Exhibit 3's six workstreams, if any, would have prevented Exhibit 6's overruns — and what does your answer imply about what Khaai should be building?
  4. The approved envelope is ₹1.20 crore against a ₹163.8 lakh proposal, and Annexure C lets Girvaan take the platform in-house after year three. Is Girvaan then the wrong beachhead, or the right one on different terms?
  5. Each of Suchit, Ekansh, Yuvraj, Elakshi, Saumil and Lohit holds a position their incentives reward. What would each decide with incentives swapped, and which reconstruction persuades you?
  6. What should Leela do at 7.30 on Monday — not in principle, but as an instruction her team can act on before 16 October? And what would she tell the board in March about Khaai's ceiling, on what evidence?

At twenty to two, Leela closed the tender and opened the February 2021 minute instead: four sentences, written by her, in the tone of someone certain they were being disciplined rather than expedient. She thought about Sohini's last line on the clarification call, and about Fjordline's eight plants being a reference in a language no Indian procurement officer reads. Outside, on the Kosi, a plant her company had watched for eight years ran at full load with nobody awake to see it.

Crossing the Chasm at Tejas Diagnostics Cloud

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Go-to-Market & Launch · Case20

1. Opening

Monday, 28 September 2026, 9 a.m., Tejas Diagnostics Cloud's office on Bedi Bunder Road, Jamnagar. Umang Chandnani, co-founder and chief product officer, read the RFP from Saurashtra Precision Diagnostics for the third time. The chain ran 400 sample-collection centres across Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra and wanted a single laboratory information system, or LIS, replacing the spreadsheets and decade-old desktop software its labs used today. The response was due by 5 p.m. on 19 October, three weeks out, in the stretch of the calendar when Navratri and Dussehra would thin out engineering and support staff alike. Umang had to recommend to the founding team by Friday whether Tejas would chase the deal as written, decline it, or propose something narrower — a choice shaping which customer Tejas built its product for over the next three years.

2. Company background

Umang and his co-founder had started Tejas Diagnostics Cloud in 2019 to sell a cloud-based LIS to independently owned pathology chains — businesses run by a single pathologist-promoter with five to forty collection centres in a Tier 2 or Tier 3 town, keeping records and billing in Excel and WhatsApp. Tejas gave them barcode-tracked samples, digital reports, UPI-linked billing and a patient app, priced low enough that an owner could approve it without a board. Word travelled through pathologist associations in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra faster than any sales campaign, and by September 2026 Tejas had 148 lab-chain customers, generating ₹18.60 crore in annual recurring revenue, detailed by segment in Exhibit 1. Tejas ran regional support desks out of Bhuj and Porbandar besides Jamnagar. Its competitors were not the giants — Dr Lal PathLabs, Metropolis Healthcare, SRL Diagnostics and Thyrocare all ran in-house systems — but a scatter of small LIS vendors, including Rachna Lab Systems, chasing the same owner-run labs Tejas already served well.

3. The situation

Two forces had converged on Umang's desk. First, the National Health Authority's push to link every lab report to a patient's Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission health ID, alongside NABL accreditation norms and DPDP Act data-localisation expectations, meant large chains needed one auditable system, integrated with hospital HIS platforms — their LIS could no longer be an afterthought. Second, pipeline data compiled by Omkar Chugh, the Toronto-based analytics lead, showed the pattern in Exhibit 2: a much higher win rate among small independent chains than among large multi-state ones — evidence, in Omkar's reading, of a genuine chasm, not a sales-execution problem. Saurashtra Precision Diagnostics was the first chain of real scale to put that gap in writing: its RFP asked for full ABDM and hospital-HIS integration, a named support SLA, and two reference customers of comparable size, none of which the early-adopter playbook had ever required. Bina Advani, running customer success from Singapore, already stretched thin on a smaller pilot for a Dubai-based hospital group, warned that anything pulling engineering attention from the core product would be felt by Segment A first.

6. The options

  1. Commit fully to the 400-centre rollout. Accept the RFP as written, staff a six-engineer pod for five months, and deliver the full integration on Saurashtra's timeline. Upside: a marquee reference, ₹85 lakh in fees, ARR ramping to ₹80 lakh by Year 3 (Exhibit 3). Cost: the pod is off-roadmap for five months, the anomaly-flagging release slips, and Bina's estimated ₹27–36 lakh of at-risk ARR sits against a Year 1 margin of only ₹19 lakh.
  2. Decline the RFP and stay in the early-adopter lane. Tell Saurashtra Tejas is not ready, keep the pod on Segment A and B, and pursue mid-size regional chains instead. Upside: protects the ₹1,860 lakh ARR base and the 30% Segment A win rate, avoids execution risk. Cost: cedes the large-chain segment, worth ₹204 lakh of ARR already, to Rachna Lab Systems or in-house builds, and caps growth at the Segment A/B ceiling.
  3. Negotiate a scoped Gujarat-only pilot. Offer the Year 1 plan from Exhibit 3 alone — 100 centres, a three-engineer pod for three months — with the remaining 300 contingent on the pilot meeting agreed SLAs. Upside: bounded cost of ₹19.8 lakh (3 × 3 × ₹2.2 lakh) against a pro-rated fee of ₹21.25 lakh (₹85 lakh × 100/400), no roadmap slip, a reusable playbook. Cost: slower revenue capture, and the risk Saurashtra takes its full RFP to a competitor willing to commit outright.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Saurashtra's RFP ask for that none of Tejas's 128 Segment A customers ever asked for — and how does Moore's "whole product" idea explain that gap?
  2. What does the pattern in Exhibit 2 tell Umang about whether Tejas has a sales-execution problem or a genuine chasm between early adopters and the mainstream?
  3. Using Exhibits 1 and 3, weigh the three options: which one protects the existing business while giving Tejas a real foothold in the mainstream segment?
  4. If Umang engages Saurashtra in some form, what should he tell Bhavesh, Ishaan and Bina by Friday about scope, staffing and the churn risk to Segment A?

8. A note for the learner

This case applies Geoffrey Moore's chasm framework: early adopters buy an incomplete product because they value being first and tolerate gaps; the mainstream buys only a "whole product" — references, compliance, support — because it cannot afford to be the experiment. Exhibit 2's win-rate drop from 30% to 10% is what a chasm looks like in a pipeline, not underperformance by Bhavesh's team. A well-reasoned answer recognises that Saurashtra's requirements define "whole product" for this market; that the ₹1,860 lakh existing ARR base funds the attempt and is not expendable; and that crossing a chasm is normally done by one bounded beachhead, not the entire mainstream at once.

Option 3 is the most defensible path. It takes Moore's "bowling pin" logic literally: the Year 1 slice of Saurashtra's own RFP — 100 Gujarat centres — is already a self-contained beachhead, sized to a three-month pod that keeps the anomaly-flagging release on schedule. It converts the RFP into a referenceable large-chain deployment while capping the downside near Exhibit 3's own numbers: about ₹19.8 lakh of engineering cost against roughly ₹21.25 lakh of pro-rated fee. If the pilot meets its SLA, Tejas gains proof it can serve the mainstream and a template for the next 300 centres, without betting the core business on one account's timeline. Option 1 is defensible only if Umang is confident the pod's absence will not touch Segment A retention; Option 2 only if he accepts conceding the mainstream for good. Option 3 is the one a cautious, growth-minded product leader can take to the board without betting the company.

Crossing the Chasm

Why the customers who love you first are almost never the customers who will make you big—and what to do about the gap in between.

A Tuesday in Pune, and a graph that will not sit still

On the morning of 11 February 2026, Meera Iyer, vice president of product at Ashwath Vision Systems, sat in a glass-walled conference room in Pune's Hinjawadi tech corridor and looked at a slide she had rebuilt four times that week. Ashwath made machine-vision inspection systems—cameras, lighting rigs and a defect-detection model bundled into a single unit—that bolted onto a factory's production line and caught cracked castings, misaligned welds and undersized bores before they reached a customer. The company had forty paying plants on its books, a live case study with a marquee auto-components group, and an ARR of roughly ₹3.2 crore. Growth had been genuinely fast for eighteen months. Then, starting in the third quarter of 2025, it had gone nearly flat. New pilots kept starting. Very few kept renewing into full deployments, and the sales team's forecast for the next two quarters showed the same pattern repeating: interest, a pilot, enthusiasm, and then silence.

The board meeting was five weeks away, and the round Ashwath needed to close depended on demonstrating that the flattening was a phase, not a ceiling. Rajan Mehta, the company's co-founder and head of sales, had a theory: the forty customers who had bought so far were not a representative sample of the market Ashwath had sized in its pitch deck. They were, in his words, "the ones who wanted to be first." The next hundred plants Ashwath needed were run by production managers who did not want to be first at anything. Meera's job that week was to figure out whether Rajan was right, and if he was, what Ashwath should actually do differently—because "sell harder to the same kind of customer" was clearly not going to close the gap she was staring at.

The idea: a gap with a name

What Meera was looking at is one of the best-documented patterns in technology marketing, and it has a name precise enough to be useful: the chasm. The term comes from the consultant Geoffrey Moore, who in 1991 published a book called Crossing the Chasm, aimed at Silicon Valley hardware and software companies that kept hitting the same wall Ashwath had just hit. Moore was not inventing a new idea from nothing; he was taking an older model—the technology adoption life cycle, first described by the sociologist Everett Rogers in his 1962 book Diffusion of Innovations—and pointing out a flaw in how technology companies were using it.

Rogers's original model sorted the adopters of any new idea or product into five groups, arranged along a bell curve by how early they buy relative to everyone else: innovators, a tiny sliver of technology enthusiasts who will try almost anything new; early adopters, visionaries who buy because a new technology lets them do something strategically important before their competitors can; the early majority, pragmatists who buy once a technology is proven, supported and low-risk; the late majority, conservatives who buy only once an approach has become the default; and laggards, who adopt last if at all. Rogers drew this as a smooth, continuous curve, and for decades marketers treated the transitions between these groups as gradual—momentum simply carrying a product from one segment into the next.

Moore's contribution was to argue that for products requiring a real change in how the customer works—what he called discontinuous innovations—the curve is not smooth at all. There is a gap between early adopters and the early majority wide enough to swallow a company, because these two groups buy for almost opposite reasons. Early adopters want to be different; the early majority wants proof that they will not be foolish. A company that has only sold to the first group has, in a very real sense, not yet entered its market. That gap is the chasm. Crossing it is not a matter of selling more of the same thing more energetically; it requires a different offer, aimed at a different kind of buyer, proven through a different kind of evidence.

The sentence Meera could say in the board meeting without sounding glib: "Our first forty customers bought us because we were unusual; our next hundred will only buy us because someone just like them already trusts us—and until we can prove that, growth will keep looking like a cliff, not a slope."

How the chasm actually works

The mechanics behind that sentence are worth walking through slowly, because most of the leverage in crossing the chasm lives in steps that practitioners tend to skip past. The first step is to accept that the adopter categories are not stages a single customer passes through over time, in the way a person moves from being twenty to being thirty. They are different types of buyer, distinguished by psychology and risk tolerance, who exist simultaneously in the market. Ashwath's forty early customers were, almost without exception, plants run by engineering-trained owners or production heads who had personally decided that machine vision was the future of quality control and wanted their plant to be seen leading that shift. They tolerated an unfinished product, filed detailed bug reports, and referred Ashwath to their industry association—to other visionaries, in other words, not to the market at large.

The second step is to recognise what the early majority is actually buying, because it is not the core technology. Moore's key mechanical concept here is the whole product: the generic technology plus everything around it that a pragmatic buyer needs before they will risk their own reputation on the purchase—installation support, integration with existing systems, training, a service level agreement, and, critically, reference customers who look like them. A visionary will buy a core product and build the rest themselves, because building it themselves is part of the appeal. A pragmatist will not. If Ashwath's product, at that moment, still required a company engineer to fly out and hand-tune the lighting rig for each new line, it had a core product, not a whole product, and no volume of enthusiastic pilots would change that fact.

The third step is choosing where to point the whole product, and this is the step Moore is most associated with: picking a single, narrow beachhead segment rather than attacking the entire addressable market at once. The counter-intuitive part is that the way to cross a wide gap is to aim narrower, not broader. A company that tries to sell simultaneously to auto-component plants, pharmaceutical packaging lines and electronics assemblers spreads its limited whole-product investment—its integrations, its case studies, its trained support staff—across three audiences that do not talk to each other and do not trust each other's references. A company that picks one segment, dominates it, and only then expands is following what Moore called the bowling alley strategy: knock down the head pin, and the pins behind it—adjacent segments that watch the first one closely—fall in sequence, because references now travel within a community that actually listens to itself.

A worked pass through Ashwath's numbers

Meera's next step was to put figures against the strategy rather than describe it in the abstract, because Rajan's instinct needed to survive contact with arithmetic before it went into a board deck. Ashwath's total addressable market, as pitched to investors, was roughly 9,000 mid-sized manufacturing plants across auto components, pharmaceutical packaging, electronics assembly and general engineering in India that ran a quality-inspection step manual enough to automate. Of those, the forty paying customers were concentrated, almost by accident, in auto-component forging and casting—a niche of about 600 plants nationally, most of them clustered around Pune, Chennai and the NCR belt and organised into two active industry associations that shared supplier gossip freely.

If Ashwath tried to sell evenly across all four verticals over the next four quarters, Meera estimated—based on the pilot-to-paid conversion the sales team had actually observed outside the forging niche—a conversion rate of about 4% from qualified pilot to signed annual contract, because each vertical would see only a handful of scattered case studies with no peer plant to call for a reference check. At an average contract value of ₹9 lakh and a pipeline of 200 qualified pilots spread across all four verticals, that produced roughly 8 new logos and ₹72 lakh of new ARR for the year—not enough to change the board's read of the flattening.

Table 1 — Two go-to-market allocations of the same 200-pilot pipeline over four quarters

If instead Ashwath concentrated every pilot, every case study and every support hour on the forging-and-casting niche where it already had proof, the picture changed sharply. Word of a defect catch at one forging plant travelled, within weeks, to the association's WhatsApp group and its quarterly meet. Meera modelled a conversion rate of 22% under that concentration—still far from certain, but grounded in what the existing forty accounts had actually shown when a prospect visited a working reference site rather than reading a deck. Run against the same 200-pilot pipeline, narrowed to plants inside the 600-plant niche, that produced 26 new logos and ₹2.34 crore of new ARR, more than triple the spread-thin outcome from the identical amount of sales effort. A second pass, tightening the target further to the 100 largest forging and casting plants—the ones whose adoption other plants in the niche would actually notice—pushed the conversion rate to roughly 30%, produced fewer absolute logos from a smaller qualified pool, but delivered 18% penetration of the entire niche within a year, which is closer to the dominant share a beachhead strategy is meant to produce before expansion into an adjacent vertical, such as pharmaceutical packaging, becomes credible.

The arithmetic does not prove the beachhead will work; it shows why the instinct to "sell to everyone who will take a meeting" was quietly destroying the very reference density the early majority needed to see before buying at all.

Nuances a learner has to sit with

The chasm is segment-specific, not company-wide

A company can be well past the chasm in one segment and still stuck on the visionary side in every other segment it has entered. Ashwath was, by Meera's read, close to crossing in forging and casting and nowhere near crossing in electronics assembly, where it had exactly two logos and no peer references at all. Treating "Ashwath" as a single point on the adoption curve, rather than plotting each vertical separately, was the analytical mistake that had made the flat topline look like one problem instead of two very different ones.

Psychographics, not demographics or company size

It is tempting to define "early adopter" and "pragmatist" by firm size or industry, but Moore's categories are about risk posture and motive for buying, which cut across those lines. A large plant with an owner who wants to be first is still a visionary buyer; a small workshop that will only act once its trade association has vetted a vendor is still a pragmatist. Segmenting a target list by revenue band without checking the buyer's actual psychology will misclassify a meaningful share of prospects.

"Whole product" is a moving target, not a checklist you finish once

The whole product a forging plant needed in 2026—local installation support, a service contract in Hindi and Marathi, integration with a specific PLC brand common in that niche—is not the whole product a pharmaceutical packaging line will need later. Crossing the chasm in a new segment usually means assembling a new whole product, even if the core technology does not change at all.

Do not confuse a big logo with a crossed chasm

Landing one large, famous account is often mistaken for proof that the mainstream has arrived, but a single marquee logo bought by an unusually risk-tolerant executive inside a large company is still a visionary sale. The test is not the size of the customer; it is whether other, similar buyers cite that customer as their reason for trusting the product.

The chasm applies to discontinuous innovations, not every product

Moore's model was built for products that ask the customer to change a process or take on switching risk. An incrementally better version of a product customers already understand—a faster payments gateway, a cheaper accounting tool—often does not face a chasm of the same width, because the early majority does not need to be persuaded that the category itself is safe. Applying full chasm-crossing tactics to a low-risk, easily understood upgrade is over-engineering the go-to-market problem.

Bowling alley versus big bang is a real choice, not a formality

Some founders read "pick a beachhead" as a box to check before reverting to broad selling the moment the board asks about total addressable market. The bowling alley strategy only works if the company is willing to say no to qualified revenue outside the chosen niche for long enough to build genuine reference density inside it—often two to four quarters longer than feels comfortable.

Crossing the chasm is not the end of the story

Moore's later work described what comes after a successful crossing as the tornado: a period of explosive, less-differentiated demand once the early majority accepts a category, followed eventually by a mainstream market where competition shifts to price and distribution. The chasm framework tells a team how to get in the door; it says very little about how to compete once the door is wide open, which is a different set of problems the reader will meet elsewhere in this course.

What the model cannot tell you

The framework does not tell Meera which of Ashwath's four verticals is the right beachhead, how large the whole-product investment needs to be, or how long the crossing will actually take—those require market research, customer interviews and judgment the model cannot supply. It is a diagnostic lens for interpreting a stalled pipeline, not a formula that outputs a segment name.

Consumer, B2B and marketplace variants—and the early-stage-versus-scale difference

The chasm was first described for enterprise technology, and it remains sharpest there because B2B buyers are professionally accountable for the risk of a bad purchase in a way that makes reference-checking almost mandatory; a plant manager who champions a failed vendor answers for it in his next performance review. Consumer products face a related but gentler version of the same gap: early adopters buy a new app because novelty itself has value to them, while the mainstream consumer needs social proof—a friend using it, a feature written up in the press, an app-store rating above a threshold—rather than a formal whole product with a service level agreement. The gap is often narrower and crossed faster in consumer markets because the cost of trying and abandoning a product is lower, but it is not absent, which is why many well-funded consumer apps with devoted early users still fail to reach a mass audience.

Marketplaces add a third wrinkle, because they have two sides that can each sit in different places on the curve at once. A marketplace can have a fully crossed chasm on the supply side—hundreds of mainstream sellers listing routinely—while still being stuck with only visionary buyers on the demand side, or the reverse, and the beachhead strategy has to be applied separately to each side, often starting with whichever side is scarcer. For a company at Ashwath's stage, the beachhead choice is close to existential, because a wrong niche wastes months the company may not have. A larger, well-capitalised company crossing a chasm in a new product line has more room to run two or three beachhead experiments in parallel and kill the ones that do not show reference density, a luxury Meera's forty-account, single-runway company did not have.

Common mistakes, and how to catch them early

The first mistake is chasing every qualified lead regardless of segment, which looks from the outside like a healthy, full pipeline and a sales team that is "not leaving anything on the table." The underlying misunderstanding is treating pipeline volume as the scarce resource, when the scarce resource is reference density inside a coherent community of buyers who talk to each other. The cheapest diagnostic is to sort the existing customer list by segment and ask how many of them can actually name another customer in the same segment when asked for a reference—if the answer is close to zero, the pipeline is wide and shallow no matter how large it looks.

The second mistake is declaring the core technology "done" and moving straight to broad marketing spend before the whole product exists. The symptom is a marketing team generating leads that sales cannot close because installation, integration or support keeps surfacing as the deal-breaker in the same three or four ways, deal after deal. The fix is to log the actual reason each pragmatist prospect walks away, which almost always reveals a short, repeatable list of whole-product gaps rather than a pricing problem.

The third mistake is mistaking a single large or famous logo for evidence the chasm has been crossed, discussed above as a nuance but common enough to also be a mistake in its own right. The diagnostic is simple: ask whether the next five prospects in the pipeline cite that logo unprompted as their reason for taking the meeting. If they do not know the account exists, it has not yet done any chasm-crossing work for the company, however good it looks in a pitch deck.

The fourth mistake is abandoning a beachhead too early because growth inside it looks slow next to the total market size cited in the pitch deck, which confuses depth with speed. The underlying error is applying big-market thinking to a small-market tactic; the fix is to track penetration of the chosen niche, not absolute logo count, as the leading indicator of whether the strategy is working.

What good looks like

Picture a company in the same position as Ashwath a year later, having made the beachhead choice deliberately. It has said no, in writing, to sales opportunities in pharmaceutical packaging and electronics assembly for two straight quarters, even when a plant in those verticals came asking. It has hired one systems-integration partner, in this telling a Pune-based firm called Akshita Systems Integrators, specifically to handle installation and PLC integration for forging and casting plants, turning a bespoke engineering task into a standard, priced service line that a pragmatist buyer can budget for in advance. It has built a reference programme deliberately, not accidentally: three named forging-plant customers who agree to host site visits, a joint presentation at the industry association's quarterly meet, and a one-page case study with real defect-catch numbers rather than marketing language. Penetration of the 600-plant niche has moved from under 7% to past 20%, and—this is the tell that the chasm has actually been crossed, not merely approached—new prospects in the niche are arriving having already spoken to an existing customer, without the sales team arranging the introduction. Only once that pattern is visible does the company open a second beachhead, using the same playbook rather than assuming the first crossing taught the market to trust the brand in general.

What Meera decided, and two questions to sit with

In the board meeting five weeks later, Meera presented Table 1 alongside Figure 1 and recommended that Ashwath commit, for the next two quarters, to selling only into the forging-and-casting niche, formalise the partnership with Akshita Systems Integrators to close the whole-product gap, and build the three-reference-site programme before spending another rupee on marketing outside that niche. Rajan's instinct had been directionally right; the numbers gave the board a reason to accept a strategy that, described only in words, would have sounded like retreating from the very market size the fundraising pitch depended on. The board approved a narrower, twelve-month plan instead of the broader eighteen-month plan originally proposed, betting that a proven 20% share of a real niche would raise the next round more credibly than a thin presence across four.

What Meera needed to learn next, and what this page does not cover, is how the story continues once a beachhead is actually won: how a company manages the transition from bowling alley into the faster, less personal, more competitive tornado phase, and how positioning and pricing typically have to change again once the customer in front of the sales team is no longer a pragmatist deciding whether to trust the category, but a conservative buyer who has never doubted it. Two questions are worth sitting with before that next reading. First, for a product you know well, can you name the specific whole-product gap that is currently costing it pragmatist customers, as distinct from a feature gap the visionaries never minded? Second, if you had to choose one beachhead segment and say no to every qualified lead outside it for six months, which segment would you choose, and what evidence would convince you, within that six months, that you had chosen wrong?

Crossing the Chasm

The gap between the early adopters and the mainstream is not a gap in the market. It is a gap in the information channel between two populations of buyers — and that reframing changes almost every decision a go-to-market team makes about it.

1Two rooms, one quarter, the same shape of problem

On 4 March 2026, in a first-floor office above a dyeing-chemical distributor on Surat's Udhna-Magdalla road, Sudha Raghavan pinned a printout of her own board deck to the wall and drew a red circle around a single line. Raghavan was chief executive of Bhagirathi Water Systems, a five-year-old company that sold a sensor-and-software package for continuous effluent monitoring: a hardware stack — pH, chemical oxygen demand proxy, total dissolved solids, flow — mounted at the outlet of a textile dyeing unit, wired to a dosing controller, and paired with a subscription dashboard that told the plant chemist how to trim reagent consumption and kept an immutable record for the state pollution control board. Hardware sold at ₹6.8 lakh per site; the software ran at ₹1.4 lakh a year, and after the first year most sites also bought a service contract worth another ₹60,000. Bhagirathi had 61 live sites and an annual recurring revenue of about ₹2.7 crore, and it was raising ₹18 crore on the argument that continuous monitoring was becoming the default in Indian process industry, which, in the direction of travel set by the Central Pollution Control Board and the state boards, it plainly was.

The circled line said: pilot-to-paid conversion, Surat 38%, outside Surat 6%. Forty-seven of the 61 sites sat within eighteen kilometres of Raghavan's office. The other fourteen were scattered across Pali, Tiruppur, Ahmedabad and one pharmaceutical park near Ankleshwar. The company had run 44 qualified pilots outside Surat in the previous four quarters and closed three. Her vice-president of sales, Arvind Pillai, read that as a coverage problem: too few feet on the ground in Tamil Nadu and Rajasthan. Raghavan read it as something more uncomfortable. Within Surat, a dyeing unit that was considering Bhagirathi could telephone four or five other units that already used it, most of them members of the same common effluent treatment plant association, several of them owned by families that intermarried. Outside Surat, that prospect could telephone nobody. The product was identical. The evidence available to the buyer was not.

Eleven hundred kilometres south, on 19 March, Ipsita Banerjee was making a different version of the same argument to a different room. Banerjee was head of product at Bhanumati Systems, a Bengaluru company two and a half years old, building an AI agent that reconciled input tax credit — matching a company's purchase ledger against the auto-populated GSTR-2B statement from the GST Network, flagging mismatches, drafting the supplier follow-up, and preparing a defensible working paper for the statutory auditor. The product was AI-native in the strict sense: without a large language model reading messy invoice PDFs and half-structured vendor emails, it would not exist. Adoption looked, on one axis, spectacular. Bhanumati had 3,100 free workspaces, 190 paying teams at ₹24,000 a year, and six enterprise contracts averaging ₹38 lakh. Total ARR was ₹2.74 crore. The free-tier graph went up and to the right with the pleasing smoothness that makes investors relax.

Banerjee's discomfort was in the second-order numbers. The six enterprise deals had taken a median of 7.5 months from first contact to signature and had each absorbed between 180 and 340 hours of solution engineering, which put gross margin on that cohort at 38% against the 79% the self-serve tier earned. Five of the six had begun as a free workspace opened by an assistant manager inside the buying company — classic bottom-up entry. But when Banerjee's team asked each enterprise buyer, in the win-loss interview, which other companies' experience had informed their decision, the answer in all six cases was: none that they could name. Two chief financial officers had asked whether any listed manufacturer of comparable size was running the product on its statutory filings. Neither had been given a name. Both had signed anyway, on the strength of an internal champion who was willing to spend personal credibility. Banerjee's question to her founders was blunt: were those six wins evidence that Bhanumati had entered the mainstream market, or evidence that it had found six unusually brave people?

Raghavan and Banerjee sell different things to different buyers through different motions. Yet their problems have the same structure, and the framework that names that structure is forty years old and much less well understood than its popularity suggests.

2The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

Start with a precise definition, because the loose one causes most of the damage. The chasm is a discontinuity in the adoption of a discontinuous innovation: a period in which sales growth stalls or reverses after the innovation has saturated the population of buyers who adopt on the basis of their own judgement, and before it has begun to propagate among the much larger population of buyers who adopt on the basis of other buyers' experience. The two populations are distinguished not by size, wealth, industry or technical literacy, but by what counts as evidence to them. That is the whole of it. Everything else — beachheads, whole products, reference programmes, bowling alleys — is a set of tactics derived from that one asymmetry.

The intellectual history runs through three distinct traditions that are usually conflated. The first is sociological: Everett Rogers's Diffusion of Innovations (1962), which synthesised several hundred empirical diffusion studies, most famously Ryan and Gross's 1943 work on hybrid seed corn adoption among Iowa farmers, and produced the five adopter categories — innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards — carved out of a normal distribution at fixed standard-deviation boundaries. Rogers's categories were descriptive statistics applied after the fact, not a causal theory of stalls, and Rogers himself emphasised the continuity of the process, mediated by opinion leaders who sat inside the social system rather than outside it.

The second tradition is quantitative: Frank Bass's 1969 model, which expresses the number of new adopters in a period as (p + q·F)·(m − N), where m is the ultimate market size, N the cumulative adopters, F = N/m the penetration fraction, p the coefficient of innovation (external influence: advertising, regulation, the buyer's own judgement) and q the coefficient of imitation (internal influence: word of mouth from prior adopters). The Bass model fits historical category diffusion remarkably well and is still the workhorse of forecasting practice. Critically, in its single-segment form it produces a smooth, single-peaked curve. It cannot produce a stall. Anyone who has looked at real sales data knows stalls happen.

The third tradition is practitioner-strategic: Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm (1991), written out of consulting work with Silicon Valley enterprise-technology firms, which asserted that the stall is not an accident but a structural feature of the adoption curve for discontinuous innovations, and prescribed a remedy — concentrate all resources on a single beachhead segment, assemble the whole product that segment needs, dominate it, and use it as the launch point for adjacent segments. Moore's case for the discontinuity was psychographic: visionaries buy a dream and tolerate an incomplete product; pragmatists buy a solution and require references from people like themselves; and a visionary reference is worthless to a pragmatist, because the pragmatist regards the visionary as reckless.

A fourth strand — the most important one for anyone who wants to referee arguments about this topic — came out of academic marketing science in the early 2000s. Jacob Goldenberg, Barak Libai and Eitan Muller examined the sales histories of a large set of new product categories and found that a substantial minority, on the order of a third to a half depending on how strictly the pattern is defined, exhibited a saddle: a sustained trough after an initial peak, followed by recovery to a higher level. That is the empirical footprint the chasm would leave. But their explanation was not psychographic. It was informational and structural: a market composed of two sub-populations with strong word-of-mouth within each and weak word-of-mouth between them will, under a two-segment Bass process, mechanically produce a saddle, with no need for any claim about buyer personality at all. The first segment saturates, its internal cascade exhausts itself, and the second segment has not yet accumulated enough internal adopters to bootstrap its own cascade. If cross-segment influence is strong enough, the saddle disappears.

The proposition this page argues: the chasm is best modelled not as a psychological gap between two kinds of person but as a low cross-segment influence coefficient in an information channel. Every classical prescription is then derivable rather than doctrinal — and, more usefully, becomes measurable, substitutable, and occasionally unnecessary.

That reframing matters because it tells you what the schools actually disagree about. Set out the propositions each would sign:

The Moore-orthodox position signs: for discontinuous innovations, the stall is predictable; the only reliable crossing mechanism is segment concentration until reference density is self-sustaining; total addressable market is irrelevant during the crossing and actively harmful as a management metric. It does not sign that the stall is inevitable for every product, nor that a company must be small to face it.

The diffusion-modelling position (Bass descendants, the saddle literature, Tellis and colleagues on cross-country takeoff) signs: stalls are a property of market structure and information flow, are forecastable from the parameters, and can be addressed either by increasing cross-segment influence or simply by surviving the trough, because in many categories the second segment's cascade eventually ignites on its own. It does not sign that narrow segment focus is always the efficient response — sometimes seeding the second segment's own opinion leaders directly dominates.

The distribution-first position (blitzscaling in its Hoffman formulation, and the winner-take-most view of platform competition) signs: in markets with strong network effects or steep supply-side scale economies, deliberately restricting your served market hands the category to a competitor who did not restrict theirs; speed of coverage beats depth of reference. It does not sign that references are unimportant — only that they can be bought with capital and manufactured with brand faster than they can be grown organically inside one niche.

The product-led-growth position signs: when the unit of adoption is an individual rather than an institution, the pragmatist's risk calculus collapses, because trying the product costs nothing and commits nobody; the chasm was an artifact of an era in which evaluating software required a capital request. It does not sign that institutional risk disappears — and Bhanumati's six CFOs are the counter-evidence.

The category-design position (the Play Bigger school) signs: the binding constraint is not reference density but category legibility — buyers cannot buy what they have no name or budget line for; the crossing is won by defining the problem publicly so that a budget category comes into existence. It does not sign that narrowing is wrong, but it treats narrowing as a communications decision rather than a resource-allocation one.

The sceptical sales-execution position (visible in the writing of practitioners such as Andy Rachleff on market pull and in most operating-metric traditions) signs the sharpest claim of all: most companies that declare themselves to be in a chasm are in fact companies without product-market fit, or with a sales process that has never been instrumented; "the chasm" is the most flattering available explanation for a stall and is therefore over-diagnosed. It does not deny the phenomenon; it denies the base rate.

An expert holds all six in mind and asks which one the data in front of them can distinguish. That is what the rest of this page is for.

3Mechanics in depth: what the crossing actually consists of

The quantitative core, worked

Take Bhagirathi's market and model it properly. Segment one — call it the self-evidencing segment — is the set of dyeing units run by owners with in-house chemical engineering capability who will evaluate a monitoring system on its physics and their own trial data. Raghavan's team estimated it at roughly 90 units nationally, of which Bhagirathi had 48. Segment two is the mainstream: about 1,450 comparable dyeing and processing units that will install continuous monitoring when their state board, their CETP, their lender or their brand customer requires it, and who will choose a vendor the way they choose a boiler supplier — by asking three peers.

Run a two-segment Bass process with plausible parameters. For segment one, p₁ = 0.06 (these buyers respond to technical publications and their own judgement) and q₁ = 0.50 (they talk to each other constantly). For segment two, p₂ = 0.004 — almost nobody in this population adopts on external stimulus alone — and internal imitation q₂ = 0.90, which is high, because once three units on a street have a system the fourth will follow quickly. The crucial parameter is the cross-segment coefficient qc: the weight segment two places on segment one's adoption. Raghavan's honest estimate was 0.05. A Surat dyeing house that had invested in its own effluent chemistry was, to the mainstream unit in Pali, a different animal in a different market with different economics and a proprietor with a reputation for expensive enthusiasms.

Simulate that annually and the shape is unmistakable. Segment one contributes about 8 adoptions in year one, 19 in year two, 22 in year three, and then falls away as it saturates: 11 in year four, 5 in year five. Segment two, driven only by p₂ plus a whisper of qc, contributes 6, 9, 12, 16 and 21 across the same years. Total annual sales therefore run 14, 28, 34, 27, 26 — a peak in year three and a two-year trough, precisely the saddle Raghavan was living through, and precisely the graph that makes a board ask whether the market is smaller than the deck claimed.

Now change one number. Hold everything else constant and raise qc from 0.05 to 0.35. Segment two's trajectory becomes 7, 14, 26, 44 and 68, and total sales run 15, 33, 48, 55, 73. No trough. No chasm. The product did not change, the price did not change, the sales headcount did not change. What changed is how much weight a mainstream buyer places on an early-segment adopter's experience.

This is the single most useful thing in the topic, and it is not how the framework is usually taught. Crossing the chasm is an engineering problem on qc. Every classical tactic is a way of raising it, and once you see that, you can invent tactics the books do not list, and you can tell when a tactic is failing because it is not touching the coefficient.

The reference-density arithmetic that sits under beachhead strategy

Why does concentration work? Because the probability that a mainstream prospect can find a credible peer reference is a non-linear function of your share of their segment, not of your absolute customer count. Model it simply: let s be your share of the segment, r the fraction of your customers who are genuinely referenceable (willing to take a call, permitted by their legal team, still happy), and k the number of peers a typical prospect consults before committing. The chance the prospect hears about you from at least one peer is 1 − (1 − r·s)k.

Third, k is set by the buyer's risk, not by you, and it rises with the consequences of being wrong — which is why regulated and safety-critical purchases feel so much harder: the same share buys less coverage when k is 10 rather than 3.
